### C-R1-01 | Scroll introduction sets political–biographical frame
**Claim:** Goldingay holds that Jer 1:1–3 supplies the key background: words of Jeremiah ben Hilkiah, priest of Anathoth in Benjamin; Yahweh’s message spanning Josiah’s thirteenth year through the end of Zedekiah’s eleventh year and Jerusalem’s exile in the fifth month.
**Quote:** “The words of Jeremiah ben Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin, to whom Yahweh’s message came in the time of Josiah ben Amon King of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign, and came in the time of Jehoiakim ben Josiah King of Judah, until the ending of the eleventh year of Zedekiah ben Josiah King of Judah, until the exile of Jerusalem in the fifth month.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 1–7 (I. Background; citation of 1:1–3)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

---

### C-R1-02 | Birth under Manasseh; Assyrian and “Canaanite” cultic context
**Claim:** Goldingay places Jeremiah’s birth in Manasseh’s reign (687–642 BC), when Judah was an Assyrian tribute state and Manasseh allowed Jerusalem worship to accommodate Assyrian deities alongside continuing traditional (“Canaanite”) spirituality.
**Quote:** “Jeremiah was born during the reign of Manasseh in Judah (687–642 BC)…. One consequence was that Manasseh allowed worship in Jerusalem to take account of Assyrian understandings of the gods and worship practices. In addition, traditional (“Canaanite”) understandings of the gods and related aspects of spirituality continued to be influential in Jerusalem and in people’s everyday lives.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 15–16 (I.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

---

### C-R1-03 | Josiah’s reformation, Torah scroll, and Jeremiah’s 626 commission
**Claim:** Goldingay links declining Assyrian power with Josiah’s religious and political reforms; the 622 temple “Torah scroll” (likely some form of Deuteronomy) came just after Yahweh’s commission of Jeremiah in 626, near Ashurbanipal’s death and Nabopolassar’s rise.
**Quote:** “The discovery came just after Yahweh’s commission of Jeremiah in 626, which was also about the time when Ashurbanipal, the last great king of Assyria, died, and when Nabopolassar, the first great Neo-Babylonian king, asserted control of Babylon…. Overlaps between these reforms and Deuteronomy suggest that the scroll was some form of what we know as Deuteronomy.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 17–18 (I.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

---

### C-R1-04 | Three kings and the fall as the narrative spine
**Claim:** Goldingay treats the political story holding the Jeremiah scroll’s narrative as that of Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah, followed by Jerusalem’s fall and aftershocks at Mizpah; Jehoahaz and Jehoiachin are unmentioned in 1:1–3 though historically significant.
**Quote:** “The political story that holds together the narrative implied by the Jeremiah scroll is thus the story of three kings, Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah, followed by the fall of Jerusalem and the aftershocks in Mizpah, of which we will read in Jeremiah.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 19–25 (I.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

---

### C-R1-05 | “Yahweh’s message came”: dictation, put-in-mouth, and cabinet models
**Claim:** Goldingay argues that the introduction requires readers to accept that Jeremiah’s words are Yahweh’s “message/word” that “happened” (hāyâ) to him, via multiple models: audible or interior speech; dictation from Yahweh’s mouth; Yahweh putting words in Jeremiah’s mouth (1:9; cf. Deut 18:18) leaving formulation partly to Jeremiah; and standing in Yahweh’s cabinet (23:21–22).
**Quote:** “The words of Jeremiah given in this historical context also comprise the ‘message,’ more literally the ‘word,’ of Yahweh that came to Jeremiah…. More literally, the message ‘happened’ (hāyâ) to Jeremiah…. Yahweh also touches Jeremiah’s mouth and says he is putting his words in Jeremiah’s mouth (1:9), which suggests a different model from dictation…. Jeremiah later suggests yet another model…. The difference between him and other prophets is that he has stood in Yahweh’s cabinet (23:21–22).”
**Locus:** slice ll. 31–42 (I.B)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

---

### C-R1-06 | “Words” of Jeremiah may include acts; protest is part of the message
**Claim:** Goldingay notes that dibrê yirmәyāhû could mean “acts of Jeremiah”; the scroll’s distinctive inclusion of what Jeremiah does and suffers means Yahweh’s message expresses itself in actions and experiences, and Jeremiah’s resistance (“Not me, I’m only a kid”) becomes part of the scroll’s message.
**Quote:** “The expression for ‘the words of Jeremiah’ (dibrê yirmәyāhû) could be understood to mean ‘the acts of Jeremiah’…. A distinctive feature of the Jeremiah scroll is the extent to which it relates things that Jeremiah does and things that happen to him. Yahweh’s message expresses itself in those actions and experiences.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 44–45 (I.B)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

---

### C-R1-07 | Three horizons of composition and reading
**Claim:** Goldingay posits three horizons corresponding roughly to the introduction: (1) particular delivery contexts of messages; (2) the 604 Baruch dictation (36:1–4, 32; also 30:1–2; 51:59–64 with 594 date); (3) production of an expanded scroll after 587 (from 1:1–3) with final form not before 562 (from 52:31–34).
**Quote:** “The scroll directly suggests three horizons for reading it; they correspond roughly to three horizons implied by the introduction. (1) There is the series of particular contexts in which Jeremiah delivered his messages…. (2) There is Jeremiah’s dictation of his entire message up to that point to Baruch in 604…. (3) There is the production of an expanded scroll sometime after 587… and of its final form as we have it not before 562….”
**Locus:** slice ll. 59–68 (II.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

---

### C-R1-08 | Post-587 retrospective and 585 as effective end of Jeremiah’s life in the scroll
**Claim:** Goldingay holds that the whole scroll sets individual messages against history through 587 and aftermath, so readers must hear both original speaking contexts and later retrospective significance; after about 585 in Egypt no further messages or stories enter the scroll; by 562 Jeremiah would have been at least eighty if alive.
**Quote:** “Yet the scroll as a whole sets Jeremiah’s individual messages in the context of the history that continues until the fall of Jerusalem and its aftermath…. By 562, Jeremiah would have been at least eighty, and he might have still been alive, but the last we hear of him is around 585, in Egypt. After that date, no one preserved any messages he received or told any stories about him that made it into the scroll.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 72–73 (II.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

---

### C-R1-09 | 604 scroll re-speaks old prophecies for Jehoiakim now; Jer 2–6 as heuristic rewritten core
**Claim:** Goldingay argues the 604 written scroll aimed to bring home two decades of message for that situation rather than archive original settings; he heuristically guesses Jer 2–6 represents Baruch’s subsequent rewritten scroll, while noting the finished scroll privileges no single horizon.
**Quote:** “In that scroll and context, Jeremiah need not have been concerned to anchor individual messages in their original settings…. ‘The mind of Jeremiah is fixed on the situation in 604 BC and he calls the old prophecies to mind entirely in terms of this situation.’… if Jeremiah got Baruch to put a collection of his messages into writing in 604, I am going to guess that Jer 2–6 represents Baruch’s subsequent rewritten scroll and keep that possibility in mind as a heuristic device….”
**Locus:** slice ll. 74–76 (II.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-10 | First/third person and poetry/prose do not prove multiple authors
**Claim:** Goldingay refuses to treat first-person vs. third-person speech, or poetry vs. prose, or subject-change, as decisive author-change markers; rhetorical affect differs, but the scroll lacks divergences of conviction that would force a poetry/prose author split.
**Quote:** “While first-person speech may mean that these words are Jeremiah’s own, it need not carry that implication…. Likewise, a move between poetry and prose need not signify a change in speaker or writer…. A difference between the convictions or message expressed in the prose and poetry would be more significant, but the Jeremiah scroll does not manifest divergences of this kind.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 80–82 (II.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

---

### C-R1-11 | Curators and storytellers, not “authentic” vs “inauthentic”
**Claim:** Goldingay prefers “curators and storytellers” over disciples/editors/scribes/Deuteronomists as labels; rejects “authentic/inauthentic” as a value judgment, holding that curatorial/story material can be as authentically Yahweh’s message as Jeremiah’s own words, and that inability to sort sources does not diminish the whole scroll’s authenticity.
**Quote:** “I will refer to them as the scroll’s curators and storytellers…. Storyteller and curator may be just as authentic messengers of Yahweh and interpreters of Jeremiah as Jeremiah himself…. Actually, we do not know which material came from Jeremiah, but this fact does not stop the entire scroll being authentic in the sense of the product of people who worked under God to bring his message to Judah.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 84–90 (II.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-12 | Post-587 creativity: survival manual complementing Kings
**Claim:** Goldingay imagines post-587 preservation and development of Jeremiah’s message (Mizpah, Bethel, Babylon, Egypt) analogous to Hosea/Amos after 722; the scroll provides theodicy-like rationale for Judah’s state, complements Kings, and functions as a “thick” response to disaster and “survival manual.”
**Quote:** “one may imagine that the confirmation of Jeremiah’s message by the fall of Jerusalem in 587 led some people… to think more about his message, to make sure it was preserved…. The scroll itself is then ‘a “thick” response to disaster…. It names the disaster, interprets the disaster, and portrays the prophet as a survivor of disaster.’ It is ‘a kind of survival manual.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 92–98 (II.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-13 | Gospels analogy for composition process
**Claim:** Goldingay models Jeremiah’s composition partly on the Gospels: both combine messages and stories (though framework is inverted); both interpret historical divine speech for later readers; time-spans are comparable; multiple versions exist (MT/LXX ≈ multi-Gospel situation); Mark/Matthew-Luke/John map heuristically onto 604 scroll / LXX / MT; all forms can be “authentic.”
**Quote:** “I do have a mental picture of the general compositional process, partly imagined on the basis of the possibility that the New Testament Gospels provide a plausible model…. Like the Jeremiah scroll, the Gospels combine messages and stories, though they make the story the framework for the messages whereas the Jeremiah scroll makes the messages the framework for the stories…. Perhaps Jeremiah and Baruch’s 604 scroll is a bit like Mark, LXX Jeremiah is a bit like Matthew, and MT Jeremiah is a bit like Luke.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 105–113 (II.B)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-14 | Focus on poetics of the received text, not redactional genetics
**Claim:** Goldingay declines to adjudicate chapter-development theories or prioritize “textual genetics rather than poetics”; he focuses on the curators’ presented understanding as authentic and warns that quest for prehistory risks neglecting the scroll itself.
**Quote:** “I therefore do not attempt to adjudicate over theories concerning the process whereby different chapters in the scroll developed…. I do not object to people studying ‘textual genetics rather than poetics,’ but I focus on the latter…. A focus on getting behind the Jeremiah scroll and tracing the process whereby it came into being risks ceasing to pay attention to the scroll itself….”
**Locus:** slice ll. 105–107, 124–125 (II.B)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-15 | Working reconstruction of compositional stages
**Claim:** Goldingay’s provisional picture: 626–604 messages (within Jer 2–6); 604 writing, Jehoiakim’s destruction, rewrite (Jer 2–6, perhaps annotated after 587); further messages through Jehoiakim–Zedekiah and after 587 (within 7–36, 46–51 as “many similar words,” 36:32); storytellers produce 1:4–19 and most of 26–45; curators assemble complexes and add 52:31–34 c. 560; near-final form by 550s–540s; then MT and LXXV recensions, possibly later glossed.
**Quote:** “Between 626 and 604, Yahweh was giving Jeremiah messages…. In 604, Yahweh told Jeremiah to write up all his messages…. Through the reigns of Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah, Yahweh continued to give Jeremiah messages…. In Mizpah or in Egypt, Jeremiah got Baruch to write down the further messages…. Storytellers in Mizpah or Egypt wrote the stories about Jeremiah…. Curators compiled the complexes…. They added 52:31–34 in about 560…. By the 550s or 540s, then, the scroll reached something close to the version we have.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 136–151 (II.B)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-16 | Silence on Persia as terminus ante quem for near-final form
**Claim:** Goldingay argues the scroll knows Medes as Babylon’s potential threat but not Persians/Cyrus/return/temple rebuild; it treats Jehoiachin’s release as hope-sign without Cyrus, so near-final form belongs before the late 550s–540s Persian horizon.
**Quote:** “The scroll refers to the Medes as a serious power and potential threat for Babylon… it shows no awareness of the Persians…. it refers to the release of Jehoiachin as if that were a sign of hope but shows no awareness of the accession of Cyrus…. By the 550s or 540s, then, the scroll reached something close to the version we have.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 147–149 (II.B)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-17 | Fourth horizon (Persian period) rejected as majority context of finalizing
**Claim:** Against much late 20th/early 21st-c. scholarship, Goldingay takes the minority view that finalizing belongs in the Babylonian period; Persian-period interest-group readings of Jer 24/29 etc. are not required by the text, risk circular redaction criticism, and fail language/content tests (no Persian words, Late Biblical Hebrew profile, Ezra–Nehemiah issues, or Greek-period markers).
**Quote:** “In placing the scroll’s finalizing in the Babylonian period, I take the minority opinion…. It makes no reference to anything we know about in the Persian period…. The First Testament does include material with a background in the Second Temple period… which explicitly refers to this background and includes Persian words and represents features of Late Biblical Hebrew. Jeremiah does not have these characteristics.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 159–183 (II.C)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-18 | Predominantly dystopian, not Persian-period hope literature
**Claim:** Goldingay contests claims that prophetic books (or Jeremiah) are mainly about hope; with b. Baba Batra 14b he sees the scroll as closer to being dominated by threat—a “predominantly dystopian text,” not what one would develop to meet Persian-period needs.
**Quote:** “Actually, the Jeremiah scroll is closer to being dominated by threat. B. Baba Batra 14b exaggerates only slightly in saying that ‘it is all of it the destruction’…. It is at least a ‘predominantly dystopian text,’ not the kind of text one would expect to develop to meet the needs of the Persian period.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 193–194 (II.C)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-19 | Fifth horizon: “in front of the text” readings acknowledged but secondary
**Claim:** Goldingay treats Persian ideological readings as etic “in front of the text” (paradoxically another “behind the text” quest for Second Temple communities); he accepts fifth-horizon post-structuralist/feminist/deconstructionist/intertextual work as legitimate but focuses commentary on the first three horizons and accepts the scroll’s invitation to read from Josiah to 587’s aftermath.
**Quote:** “The suggestion that the Jeremiah scroll relates to the Persian period is an interpretation that arises from a Western scholarly context…. To put it in anthropological terms, it is etic rather than emic…. Such readings informed by post-structuralism, feminism, deconstruction, and intertextuality have flourished…. In the commentary, I will refer to some exercises in interpretation that reflect the fourth and fifth horizons, but my focus will be on the first three.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 199–207 (II.D)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-20 | Background in Torah, Prophets, Psalms; Hosea marriage imagery
**Claim:** Goldingay situates Jeremiah against Israel’s sacred traditions (creation, ancestors, Sodom, exodus, wilderness, pledge, Ten Words, Moses/Samuel intercession, Shiloh) and notes especially Hosea-like husband–wife imagery for Yahweh–Israel, plausible via a Hosea scroll in Jerusalem after Samaria’s fall; Jer 3:1 alludes to Deut 24; influence with Deuteronomy, 2 Kgs 17–25, Psalms, Isa 40–55, and Ezekiel may run either way.
**Quote:** “Jeremiah’s own way of speaking about Yahweh’s relationship with Israel as like that of a husband with his wife—a relationship that laid on the wife an expectation of submission to her husband that Israel failed to fulfill—recalls the message of the Ephraimite prophet Hosea…. In his comments on that quasi-marital relationship, Jeremiah also takes up teaching from the Torah that appears in Deut 24, to which Jer 3:1 constitutes a more or less explicit reference.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 214–223 (II.E)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[divine-human-marriage]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]], [[lalleman-jeremiah-lamentations-totc]]

### C-R1-21 | Jeremiah more historical than Jonah/Ecclesiastes fictional constructs
**Claim:** Goldingay rejects treating Jeremiah as essentially a literary creation like Baruch or the Letter of Jeremiah; multiple considerations (untidy rolling corpus; unlikelihood of inventing an obscure fictional prophet; concrete historical interaction 620s–560s; past-as-basis-for-future logic; message deconstructs if pure fiction; seal/name/event connections) make a factual prophetic core likelier than pure imagination—though fact/fiction judgment affects history more than message-reception for some analogues.
**Quote:** “These considerations suggest that the Jeremiah scroll is more likely to be based on fact and to relate to an actual prophet called Jeremiah than to be purely a work of the imagination.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 230–253 (II.F)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-22 | Authorship: curators as down-to-earth authors; Jeremiah as real author
**Claim:** Goldingay states that in a literal sense authors are the curators finishing in the 550s/540s, but they aimed to transmit the real author—Jeremiah as poet, preacher, crusader, persuader.
**Quote:** “In a literal, down-to-earth sense, the authors of the Jeremiah scroll are the curators who did their work in the period that came to an end in the 550s or 540s. But they would not have seen themselves as the scroll’s authors. Their aim was to transmit the message of the real author, the prophet Jeremiah—poet, preacher, crusader, persuader.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 259–263 (III)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-23 | Jeremiah as poet: form, performance, and style
**Claim:** Goldingay characterizes First Testament prophetic poetry as bicola with complementary cola, looser rhythm than Psalms/Proverbs/Job, fondness for tricola and enjambment, hyperbolic and elliptical style; he compares prophetic chant to rap performance and describes Jeremiah’s style as staccato, multi-voiced, assonant, image-rich.
**Quote:** “The prophets were poets…. I assume that they would chant their messages like rap artists…. In general, Jeremiah’s poetic style is characterized by ‘staccato exclamations, rapid changes of scene and vantage point, frequent shifts of voice and discourse… and precision of metonymy and synecdoche.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 269–289 (III.A)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-24 | Poetry and prose complementary; “self-proclaimed Deuteronomist”
**Claim:** Goldingay holds Jeremiah would naturally use both poetry (figurative, elliptical) and prose (direct, persuasive, prolix); prose overlaps Deuteronomy and Joshua–Kings sermon style; he likes the observation that “Jeremiah was a self-proclaimed Deuteronomist,” while first-person intros signal dictation-like presentation and third-person prose intros signal curatorial mediation.
**Quote:** “Thus, the question whether Jeremiah himself could have communicated both in poetry and in prose is answered as soon as asked…. I like the observation that ‘Jeremiah was a self-proclaimed Deuteronomist.’… The former invite the hearers to take what follows as something Jeremiah is dictating…. The latter invite the hearers to take what follows as mediated by a curator.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 299–307 (III.B)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-25 | Crusader: apostasy of Judah as constant thread (not Messiah or social reform alone)
**Claim:** Goldingay argues modern assumptions (Messiah promise or social reform) cover under five percent of Jeremiah’s activity; the constant thread is Judah’s apostasy—other gods (bәʿālîm, planetary deities), child sacrifice, images of Yahweh, and ethical/political practices clashing with Yahweh even when cult is formally Yahwistic.
**Quote:** “While Jeremiah does a little of each of these things, they do not describe more than five percent of his activity. His main focus lies on challenging people to be faithful to Yahweh and not to serve other deities…. ‘The constant thread throughout the book is the apostasy of Judah.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 313–328 (III.C)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-26 | Persuader: threat and turn both aim reform; rhetoric of horror and marriage image
**Claim:** Goldingay reads even declarations of inevitable wrath as aimed to get hearers to prove him wrong; imagery (including marriage/unfaithful sisters, Jer 3) is pragmatic rhetoric of horror to reform, not mere ornament; classical devices (metonymy, catachresis, anaphora, paronomasia; rāʿâ as dire action/experience) serve persuasion.
**Quote:** “Even when he is declaring that they are incorrigible and that calamity is inevitable, he is aiming to get them to prove him wrong…. Talking in terms that come from the human experience of marriage, family, work, and politics makes it possible to bring home the nature of the relationship between Yahweh and Judah…. It is an aspect of ‘the prophets’ rhetoric of horror designed to terrify their audience into reform.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 331–343 (III.D)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[divine-human-marriage]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R1-27 | Anthologists: chains of bite-sized messages and ambiguous structure markers
**Claim:** Goldingay treats poetic units as bite-sized and linked in chains (sometimes headed “Regarding…”); transition markers (“Yahweh has said this,” “Yahweh’s affirmation,” lākēn, kî, gender/number shifts, tricola) are ambiguous and can be resumptive; structural analysis of chapters (e.g., Jer 2) is less objective than hoped and may yield complementary divisions.
**Quote:** “Jeremiah’s poetic messages are typically bite-sized…. But Jeremiah and his curators have handed down his poetic messages linked to one another in chains…. analysis of structure may turn out to be less objective than one might hope. Interpreters may thus analyze a chapter in varying but complementary ways….”

**Claim:** Goldingay finds no solid textual basis for MT as Babylonian-exile-community ideology writing off Egypt/Judah; more obvious locations for preservation/development are Egypt and Judah; if the shorter Greek base is older, it may originate in Egypt (LXX home; end-point of Jeremiah and Baruch) with MT background in Judah—possibilities only.

### C-R1-30 | Messenger model; Yahweh/Jeremiah voice often indistinct by design
**Claim:** Goldingay explains prophetic authority via the royal-messenger model (“Yahweh has said this”); Jeremiah moves between Yahweh-as-I and Yahweh-as-he; failure to mark speaker transitions is not mere error—whether Yahweh or Jeremiah speaks “doesn’t make any difference” because it is always Jeremiah speaking and always Yahweh’s message.
**Quote:** “Prophets commonly introduce their words by saying, ‘Yahweh has said this,’ which corresponds to the way a messenger might introduce a message from a king…. One is tempted to try to identify the speaker each time, but Jeremiah’s failure to mark the transitions is not simply a mistake; whether Yahweh or Jeremiah is speaking doesn’t make any difference.”

**Claim:** Goldingay insists even personal protests and experiences function as Yahweh’s message to the people; there is no indication of divine rebuke for Jeremiah’s protests; readers must ask how experiential material is designed as message.

**Claim:** Goldingay rejects the claim that Jeremiah is planless: bookended by commissioning (ch. 1) and Jerusalem’s fate (ch. 52); divides into two halves—messages then stories—with ch. 25 both concluding the first half and opening the second; tapestry is complex but not formless.

**Claim:** Goldingay divides the second half: Introduction 25; Part 3 (26–36: prophets stories; hope 30–33; reversion stories 34–36); Part 4 (37–45: last chances/calamity/Ebed-melech; aftermath/Baruch); Part 5 OAN (46 Egypt; 47–49 neighbors/distant; 50–51 Babylon); Epilogue 52.
